contents.reason: The distributive law for subgroup commutators over products of normal subgroups is used here only in the special case of a central product, where the page proves the corresponding statement about that construction directly and with the exact hypotheses it has; the general law belongs with the subgroup-commutator development.

contents.reason: This is a recognition theorem about arbitrary $p$-groups rather than a statement about extraspecial ones, and its proof needs machinery this page does not otherwise build: the Three Subgroup Lemma and the inequality $[\gamma_i,\gamma_j]\le\gamma_{i+j}$, the $\Omega_1$ and $\mho_1$ subgroups, and a $p$-rank argument about normal abelian subgroups. Craven’s own write-up leaves two steps as assertions ("the same is true in the $p$-rank 2 case"), so a faithful local proof is a research-grade reconstruction, not a transcription. The scaffold records the exact machinery so the step-3 adjudicator can decide whether to commission it.

sources.title: D. Kaur and A. Kulshrestha, Characters of real special $2$-groups (arXiv:1510.06583v1)
sources.locator: §2 "Quadratic maps and special 2-groups", pp. 2–6 in full — the section opening and §§2.1–2.3, Theorem 2.1 through Lemma 2.8

contents.name: §2 opening: a quadratic map $q:V\to W$ over a field of characteristic two, and its polar map $b_q(v,w)=q(v+w)-q(v)-q(w)$
§2 opening: the radical $\operatorname{rad}(b_q)$, a regular quadratic map, and a quadratic form as the case $W=F$
§2 opening: a special $2$-group, $\Phi(G)=[G,G]=Z(G)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^{n}$
§2.1 Quadratic maps associated to special $2$-groups: $q(xZ(G))=x^2$ is a well-defined quadratic map $G/Z(G)\to Z(G)$ whose polar map is $b_q(xZ(G),yZ(G))=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$
Theorem 2.1: a regular quadratic map with $\langle b_q(V\times V)\rangle=W$ determines a special $2$-group, unique up to isomorphism
contents.reason: This is the converse direction, rebuilding a group from a form. Its proof runs through normal $2$-cocycles and $H^2(V,W)$, and the library develops no group cohomology at any order, so neither the construction nor its uniqueness can be stated here. This page needs only the forward map from the group to its form.

contents.name: Proposition 2.2: $q_c(x)=c(x,x)$ is a quadratic map for a normal $2$-cocycle $c$, and $q_c\mapsto[c]$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Quad}(V,W)\to H^2(V,W)$
contents.reason: The bijection is a statement about the second cohomology group of an elementary abelian group with trivial coefficients. Neither its source nor its target can be written in this library, which reaches no group cohomology, and nothing on this page consumes the correspondence.

contents.name: Remark 2.3: the group $G_q$ on $V\times W$ with $(v,w)(v',w')=(v+v',c(v,v')+w+w')$, the group associated to a quadratic map
contents.reason: The multiplication is written in terms of the normal $2$-cocycle $c$ supplied by Proposition 2.2, so without that correspondence there is no operation to define. It inherits exactly the missing subject area of the two rows above rather than a missing lemma.

contents.name: §2.2 Extraspecial $2$-groups; the central product $H\circ_\Phi K=(H\times K)/N$ with $N=\langle\{(h,k)\in Z(H)\times Z(K):\Phi(h)k^{-1}=1\}\rangle$

Remark 2.4: the quadratic map of an extraspecial $2$-group is a quadratic form; $q_{D_4}(x,y)=xy$ and $q_{Q_2}(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2$; for each $n$ there are exactly two extraspecial $2$-groups of order $2^{2n+1}$, namely $D_4\circ\cdots\circ D_4$ and $Q_2\circ D_4\circ\cdots\circ D_4$

§2.3 From extraspecial to special: the transfer $s^{*}(q)=s\circ q$ along $0\ne s\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2}(W,\mathbb F_2)$, and the induced form $q_s$ on $V_s=V/\operatorname{rad}(b_{s^{*}(q)})$
contents.reason: The transfer exists to reduce a special $2$-group with a large centre to extraspecial quotients. Every group on this page has a centre of order two, so $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2}(W,\mathbb F_2)$ has one nonzero element and the construction degenerates to the identity, carrying no content here.

contents.name: Lemma 2.5: if $\operatorname{rad}(b_{s^{*}(q)})$ vanishes under $s^{*}(q)$ then $q_s:V_s\to\mathbb F_2$ is regular and $b_{q_s}$ is surjective
contents.reason: Under the degeneration recorded in the previous row $V_s=V$ and $q_s=q$, so for an extraspecial group this lemma says exactly that the commutator pairing has trivial radical, which the page proves directly. Restating it in transfer form would import the special-$2$-group apparatus for no gain.

contents.name: Remark 2.6: a real special $2$-group satisfies $s^{*}(q)(\operatorname{rad}(b_{s^{*}(q_G)}))=0$; a group is real when the classes of $x$ and $x^{-1}$ coincide for every $x$
contents.reason: Realness is a condition on conjugacy classes introduced here to control complex characters. The library develops no character theory of finite groups at any order, so the property has no consumer and no way to earn its keep on this page.

contents.name: Theorem 2.7: $G$ is real if and only if for every $v\in V$ there exists $v'\in V$ with $q(v')=q(v+v')$
contents.reason: The criterion translates realness into the quadratic map, and realness is the character-theoretic notion the previous row places outside the library. This page classifies the two isomorphism types rather than analysing conjugacy classes, so the translation has nothing to serve.

contents.name: Lemma 2.8: for $0\ne s$ the group $G_s$ associated to $q_s$ is an extraspecial $2$-group, and $V_s\cong G_s/Z(G_s)$
contents.reason: This is the patching step that assembles representations of a real special $2$-group from those of its extraspecial quotients. The page builds no representations, and $G_s$ itself is produced by the cocycle machinery of Proposition 2.2 that the library cannot express.

contents.name: Theorem 7.77 and Corollary 7.78 (the fundamental group of a connected graph is free; the universal cover of a bouquet is the Cayley tree)
contents.reason: The proof runs through maximal subtrees chosen by Zorn, subdivision, and the Seifert–van Kampen theorem applied to the realisation; the page has no realisation functor and proves the free-group tree statement combinatorially instead. The planned simplicial-tree page owns arbitrary trees and group actions on them and is where the topological route belongs.

contents.name: Corollary 7.79 and Corollary 7.80 (a group acting freely on a simplicial tree is free; Nielsen–Schreier)
contents.reason: Both rest on the covering-space argument of Theorem 7.77 or on Schreier transversals, and the scaffold that owns subgroups of free groups is the planned Schreier-rewriting page; deriving Nielsen–Schreier here would duplicate that page’s central theorem from machinery this page does not have.

contents.name: Proposition 7.81 ($F_2$ contains $F_m$ for every finite $m$ and for $m=\aleph_0$, with finite index in the finite case)
contents.reason: The finite-index statement is computed from Euler characteristics of covering graphs and the infinite-rank statement from a ping-pong argument on reduced words; neither covering graphs nor ping-pong is available here, and both are part of the free-subgroup development of the Schreier page.

contents.name: Exercise 7.82 (the word metric of a wreath product $G\wr H$)
contents.reason: Wreath products are not constructed anywhere in this library, and building the restricted wreath product with its canonical generating set purely to state a distance formula would import an entire construction with no other consumer on this page or its block.

contents.name: §7.9 closing discussion (different generating sets give non-isometric Cayley graphs; all Cayley graphs of a finite group have finite diameter)
§8.1 Definition 8.1 (quasi-isometric spaces as those containing bilipschitz equivalent separated nets)
§8.1, the notion of a separated net
Examples 8.2 (a space of finite diameter is quasi-isometric to a point; a normed $\mathbb R^n$ to $\mathbb Z^n$)
Question 8.3 and Theorem 8.4 (Burago–Kleiner: a separated net in $\mathbb R^2$ need not be bilipschitz equivalent to $\mathbb Z^2$)
contents.reason: This is a deep counterexample from a research paper, not proved in the source, and its construction uses measurable-density techniques far outside anything the library builds; recording it as established would put an unproved research theorem on the dependency spine.

contents.name: Definition 8.5 (coarse Lipschitz maps and quasi-isometric embeddings)
Example 8.6 (the floor function is coarse Lipschitz and a quasi-isometric embedding; $x\mapsto x^2$ is not)
Lemma 8.7 (a coarse Lipschitz map between word metric spaces is Lipschitz)
Lemma 8.8 (a map on a geodesic space that is bounded on $r$-close pairs is coarse Lipschitz)
contents.reason: The proof subdivides an actual geodesic into steps of length at most $r$, so it needs a geodesic source; the spaces this page handles are word metric spaces, which are only quasi-geodesic, and the corresponding statement there is the Lipschitz lemma already included. The geodesic version is the form the Švarc–Milnor argument needs on the next page.

Exercise 8.11(4) (a map at finite distance from a quasi-isometry is a quasi-isometry)

Example 8.14, Example 8.15 and Example 8.16 (the cylinder $S^n\times\mathbb R$; graphs of Lipschitz functions; the spiral map of $\mathbb R^2$)
contents.reason: Each is a computation in a Riemannian or differentiable setting: the cylinder needs a product metric on a sphere, and the spiral map is verified by pulling back the Euclidean metric in polar coordinates with a differentiability hypothesis. The library has neither Riemannian metrics nor polar-coordinate calculus on the plane at this point of the reading order.

contents.name: Proposition 8.17 (the net definition and the map definition of quasi-isometry agree)
Remark 8.18 (the choice used in Proposition 8.17 is avoidable for proper spaces)
Definition 8.19 (quasi-isometric relations, and their equivalence with quasi-isometries)
contents.reason: The relational formulation is stated through Hausdorff distances between projection fibres, so it needs the Hausdorff distance between subsets of a metric space; that notion is developed in the source’s own §2.4 and nowhere in this library, and the page already has two equivalent formulations of quasi-isometry.

§8.1, the homomorphisms $\mathrm{Isom}(X)\to QI(X)$, $G\to QI(G)$ and $VI(G)\to QI(G)$
contents.reason: Virtual isomorphism and the commensurator are defined in the source’s §5.2 and are not built here, and the statements about the kernel of $G\to QI(G)$ are proved much later in the source from centraliser results; the page can define the quasi-isometry group honestly without them.

contents.name: Definition 8.25 and Definition 8.27 (coarse embeddings; uniformly proper maps), with Lemma 8.26, Lemma 8.29, Lemma 8.30 and Corollary 8.31
contents.reason: Coarse embeddings weaken the quasi-isometric bounds to arbitrary proper distortion functions, and the accompanying lemmas are stated for geodesic or proper targets and for properly discontinuous actions. That circle of ideas is the technical core of the Švarc–Milnor lemma on the next page of this block, and separating it from that lemma would leave definitions with no theorem.

contents.name: Definition 8.32, Definition 8.33 and Proposition 8.34 (coarse uniform convergence and the coarse Arzelà–Ascoli theorem)
contents.reason: This is a compactness statement about sequences of quasi-isometries, proved from the classical Arzelà–Ascoli theorem on a net in a proper space; its consumers are the rigidity arguments of the source’s later chapters, and it is used nowhere in the Cayley graph, word metric or quasi-isometry development.
